speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I wish to point out that in Votes and Proceedings for today there is a notice of motion standing in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce returnable on Thursday next which in its main purpose has precisely the same purpose as a motion already before the house standing as order No. 13, which motion is already in the possession of the house and has been debated. As Your Honour will see, the first part of the motion, dealing with the main substance of the motion that is already before the house, is precisely the same except for minor verbal variations as the opening part of the notice now in Votes and Proceedings.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that an order cannot be placed on the order paper in this way in substitution for an order already there, nor can there be duplicating motions by the government in regard to the same subject. I submit that this is not in any way affected by the fact that there is additional material in the notice now before us. The effect of that would simply be to provide for an amendment of the motion already being debated by the house. I think it is clear that an amendment may not be made in this way. I think it is very clear that as far as proceedings are concerned nothing can be done by indirection which cannot be done directly. I think there is no question about the fact that this procedure would be ineffective, and I therefore submit to Your Honour that the notice now appearing in Votes and Proceedings should not proceed to the order paper tomorrow.

Mr. Speaker, may I support those who have already asked Your Honour to rule as to whether or not the notice of motion filed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) should be permitted to reach the order paper. I might point out, first of all, that Your Honour is required to deal with a matter of this kind under the terms of standing order 50 which reads as follows:
50. Whenever Mr. Speaker is of opinion that a motion offered to the house is contrary to the rules and privileges of parliament, he shall apprise the house thereof immediately, before putting the question thereon, and quote the standing order or authority applicable to the case.
I would draw Your Honour's attention to certain citations in addition to those that have been referred to by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). In particular I would ask you to look at citation 325 in Beauchesne's third edition which reads as follows:
A motion or amendment cannot be brought forward which is the same in substance as a question which has already been decided . . .
I would draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that this house has, by a decision of the house, already referred to the committee of the whole a resolution dealing with the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation. In other words, the house will be asked-if the present notice of motion reaches the order paper tomorrow-to take another decision similar to one that has already been taken. That is the point which the Leader of

Business of the House the Opposition made. I am merely buttressing it by reference to citation 325.
I also remind Your Honour that on Monday of this week one of the reasons that Your Honour gave for denying the motion for adjournment under standing order 26 which my leader moved on that occasion was that it anticipated a subject in connection with which a resolution was already on the order paper and which the house had already appointed for debate.
I would also remind Your Honour that on other occasions in this session and in other sessions you, sir, have produced an abundance of citations and authorities to indicate that there cannot be two debates on the same subject before the house at the same time. There is already before the house a debate on a resolution with regard to the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation. Now we have proposed for the order paper another resolution which is in part the very same as the one that is already before us.
Mr. Speaker, this is not a new issue to arise in parliament. There have been previous occasions when the government, after placing a notice of motion preceding a money bill on the order paper, has found it desirable to make a change in the terms of that motion. I have not had time since I received my copy of Votes and Proceedings only a short while ago to do all the homework I should like to do, but I have found at least one such case. It occurred in 1945. Your Honour is smiling and I think that means you have been doing your homework, too. On that occasion-I notice Your Honour now shakes his head. On that occasion Mr. Ilsley, who was then minister of finance, had introduced a resolution forecasting a bill to amend the National Housing Act. The resolution was ordered referred to the committee of the whole house on October 9, 1945.
Later, it was decided by the government that the terms of the resolution, and accordingly the terms of the bill to be based thereon, should be extended. The government did not do on that occasion what I contend it is improperly trying to do now, put on another resolution saying the same thing as the first one but adding some words. Rather Mr. Ilsley, who is now a learned justice of one of the superior courts of this country, introduced another notice of motion which was to the effect that the resolution of October 9, 1945, be amended by adding thereto certain additional words. Subsequently this resolution was referred to the committee of the whole house. It was passed by the committee of the whole house

as had been the previous resolution and accordingly a bill based upon the composite resolution was introduced.
It is in my mind that there have been other such occasions. I believe Mr. Ilsley was the mover of another bill in which the same procedure was followed. It is also in my mind that there have been bills dealing with veterans legislation where changes have been decided upon after the legislation was before the house; in some instances perhaps as a result of a recommendation of a special committee on veterans affairs, and as a result of that decision to change the bill a subsequent amending resolution has been presented to the house. I confess that with regard to these instances I am relying on my memory, not yet having had time to locate them in the records, but I think the records will confirm my memory.

The member for Winnipeg North Centre seldom declines an invitation to say a few words on procedure. I have given thought to the point which Your Honour has raised and I suggest that there are certain very real differences. In the case of the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) with regard to equal pay for equal work for women and in the case of the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) regarding small loans companies, those private bills were placed on the order paper in advance of the notices of the government bills.
It might be argued that those bills blocked the government legislation, but the answer

to that argument is that the rule books contain a provision which is known as the rule of anticipation. This rule establishes an order of priority and provides that certain legislation shall have priority over other kinds of legislation. Government bills are listed as being higher in priority than private members' bills. It is provided in the authorities for a government bill to be placed on the order paper and have priority over a private member's bill dealing with the same matter. That is precisely what has happened. I think it has been pretty well understood that since the government legislation regarding these two subjects appeared on the order paper Your Honour would not permit further debate on the private members' bills. They are now blocked by the higher priority of the government legislation.
But there is nothing anywhere in the rule books that says that there is any difference in priority between one government measure and another. I suggest that the government cannot come along and claim that its second thought has priority over its first thought and that therefore it takes precedence over the resolution already there. It seems to me that the situations are quite different. In this case the government should fall back on the procedure used in the instance to which I referred when Mr. Ilsley had the national housing bill before us and in the other instances which I hope I will be able to give if this matter comes up tomorrow.

I have always understood that, in an obvious case, that is to say where a notice of motion obviously offends the rules, it is the responsibility, in the first instance, of the Clerk of the house, and in the final instance of the Speaker of the house, to decide whether such a motion obviously out of order should be permitted to be printed, first of all in Votes and Proceedings as a notice of motion and then on the order paper of the house for the following day. My understanding is that in an obvious case that responsibility rests upon the Clerk as an officer of the house in the first instance and then on the Speaker.

As was said by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, it may be that you do not have to decide the point on the spur of the moment but in my respectful submission a decision must be made by you, Mr. Speaker, today before the contents of tomorrow's order paper go to the printer to be printed.
I wish to enlarge on the point and the reasons why I submit to you that this notice of motion appearing in Votes and Proceedings for Tuesday, May 8, is one of those cases of a notice of motion obviously out of order, so obviously out of order as to call on your part for a direction that it shall not be printed at the expense of the taxpayers of this country in breach of the rules of the house.

Business of the House are reproduced in the fourth paragraph of the new notice of motion. If we are to permit the defeat of the rule of the house embodied in citation 387 of Beauchesne, second edition, which expressly prohibits the anticipation of something that is already on the order paper by something new introduced, then, sir, all that one has to do to achieve that defeat of a well established rule of the house is simply to add a couple of new things or, for that matter, one new thing, to something that is already on the order paper, something that is not only on the order paper but has already been debated by the House of Commons and ordered to stand for further discussion at a later date. That is all that needs to be done. Just add something else and then you escape the rule with regard to anticipation.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the plain rules and well established procedures of the house are not to be defeated in a manner of that kind. It just means that it would be the simplest thing in all the world from this point on to add something to anything that is on the order paper, bring it in in that way and, if you please, put it ahead of something that is already on the order paper. Yesterday the Minister of Finance as leader of the house, in answer to a question I put to him, made it quite clear that it is the intention of the government to take this new notice of motion in priority to the resolution standing on the order paper as order No. 13. So that you have the plainest kind of attempted anticipation, taking something new ahead of something already on the order paper and in this case consisting of precisely the same resolution with the addition of two new paragraphs.


In such a case it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, if I may respectfully say so, that it is the duty of the Speaker of the house to dispose of this question today in view of the fact that the notice of motion appearing in yesterday's Votes and Proceedings is so obviously out of order as being an attempt at anticipation in relation to the notice of motion of March 15 that it is your duty to rule today that that notice of motion shall not be printed in tomorrow's order paper.

speechtext:
May I say first of all that all hon. members who have stated the point have been very helpful in citing authorities and dealing with the point quite fully. There have been several points raised. There is one, however, that I should like to see disposed of immediately. In discussing the point of order some hon. members have emphasized that their view as to why this procedure is out of order is the most obvious one. It is so obvious to them that they do not see anything else but their own view as being the obvious one. Then they go on further to say that it is the duty of the Clerk and the duty of the Speaker to decide in a certain way, as if both the Clerk and the Speaker would not be doing their duty otherwise.
I want to say immediately that I have been associated with the Clerk of the house for over seven years, as Speaker for the last three years and as Deputy Speaker and deputy chairman of committees for four years prior to 1953. In my view no one knows his duty better than the Clerk of the House of Commons. Whatever he does in his capacity as adviser to the Speaker it is not his responsibility. It is that of the Speaker and I fully accept whatever responsibility is mine.
I want to say that whenever a notice of motion goes to the order paper it is dealt with by the clerk of orders and notices, who is a different person from the Clerk of the House of Commons. The clerk of orders and notices has been a member of the staff of the house for over 30 years, has had a great deal of experience and takes a look at these motions before he puts them on the order paper. If he has any doubts he may refer to the assistant clerks, of whom there are two, or to the Clerk himself. If the Clerk has no doubt whatever these motions never come before me but if he has any doubt he may put them before me.
By quoting pages 312 and 313 of Bourinot's fourth edition the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) indicated that the officials of the house have certain duties with respect to the preparation of the order paper. There is no doubt about that fact. That is what they are there for. But someone must take the responsibility and that someone is the one who

is occupying the chair. I say again that I take full responsibility for whatever has taken place. Let us have that point clear and let us keep the officials of the house outside the argument.
Now that we are all in agreement on that particular matter, I should like to go one step further. Hon. members have objected to the notice of motion which is now on the notice paper and which normally should appear on the order paper tomorrow as a government notice of motion. They have objected to it on the ground that it anticipated a notice of motion which has already been taken up by the house and been considered in committee of the whole. I should like to inform hon. members that according to Campion at page 176, we find this. Campion deals with the rule that the same question may not be twice offered in the same session and I should like to quote this portion:
The important points in connection with this rule are:
(1)	Judgment must have been expressed. Consequently a motion which has been withdrawn, or has not been seconded, or has been superseded, may be repeated.
(2)	The rule does not apply as between the various stages of bills. The different stages are intended as so many opportunities of reconsideration. Hence decisions taken in committee may be reversed upon the report stage, and these again on consideration of Lords' amendments.
At page 202 Campion deals with bills that have to be introduced with preliminaries, namely the resolution preceding a money bill. Under the heading "Bills brought in on an order of the house", he says this:
This is the old procedure, which has been practically superseded except in the case of money bills and bills introduced under S.O. No. 12.
That is standing order No. 12 in the United Kingdom.
Bills introduced on an order may be preceded bv certain preliminary business.
Then he deals with preliminaries.
With Preliminaries.
(a) A certain class of bills, whose main object is the expenditure of money or the imposition of taxation, generally called 'money' bills, are still required to be preceded by resolutions passed in committee of the whole house and agreed to by the house on report. In this case the bill is ordered to be brought in immediately after the resolutions are agreed to.
The resolution preceding a money bill is nothing but the order for leave to introduce a bill which entails the expenditure of money. In my view it is part of the bill. A money bill has various stages and the preliminary stage, which is the resolution, is part of the set-up in the bringing in of a bill. When a bill is introduced without a resolution I ask the house the question "Has the hon. gentleman leave to introduce this bill?" The house having acceded to that
Business of the House suggestion then the Votes and Proceedings read "Ordered that the bill be introduced". Then I ask for first reading. When a money bill is introduced, it must be preceded by a resolution and once the resolution is concurred in by the house, the order is for leave to introduce the money bill. That is the position.
What is the position at the moment in this instance? A resolution is on the order paper and the order is "House again in committee of the whole on a certain proposed resolution". I stress the word "proposed" because I submit to hon. members this consideration: When does a resolution become a resolution? After it has come out of the committee of the whole. As long as it is in committee of the whole and until it is reported it is only a proposed resolution. As a matter of fact, as hon. members know, a motion preceding a money bill may be amended in committee and it is not even reported with amendments when it is reported. A resolution may be amended in committee of the whole provided the terms of reference of the royal recommendation may allow the amendment in committee. Otherwise a new royal recommendation is necessary. In this case we have on the order paper "House again in committee of the whole on a certain proposed resolution" which deals with certain matters. We now have on the notice paper a certain proposed resolution which deals with the same subject matter as does the proposed resolution which is in committee of the whole, plus other matters which require the royal recommendation because of the financial initiative of the crown.
ft hon. members will bear with me, I would ask them to look at page 499 of May's fifteenth edition. There they will find this: There is no rule or custom which restrains the presentation of two or more bills relating to the same subject, and containing similar provisions. But if a decision of the house has already been taken on one such bill, for example, if the bill has been given or refused a second reading the other is not proceeded with if it contains 'substantially the same provisions, and such a bill could not have been introduced on a motion for leave. But if a bill is withdrawn, after having made progress, another bill with the same objects may be proceeded with.
This is complemented by what appears in Bourinot at page 548 where Bourinot quotes a reference to the English authorities which is as follows:
"Whilst a bill is still pending, and until it is completely disposed of, there is nothing whatever to prevent another bill for the same object being introduced."
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), when I asked him

But with respect to the point that the rule of anticipation has established a scale of values, may I say that the scale of values does not apply as between government bills and private members' bills. It applies as to the various stages along the way of a certain bill as against another which may not have advanced so far.
What was the page I quoted a moment ago about the rule of anticipation? I suppose that, while I am looking for this reference, it is for hon. members a pleasant interlude in which to think over what they have said and what I have said.
We will look at the scale of values which has been established by Campion at page 178. He says:
The anticipation rule, which forbids discussion on a matter standing on the paper being forestalled, is dependent on the same principle as that which forbids the same question being twice raised in the same session. In applying the anticipation rule preference is given to the discussion which leads to the most effective result, and this has established a descending scale of values for discussions-bills, motions, amendments, etc. Thus a bill or other order of the day must not be anticipated by (or more shortly "blocks") discussion of a motion, amendment, or subject raised on another motion, such as that for the adjournment of the house.
While it applies between the various stages of a bill, there is no order of priority as between government bills and private members' bills. I am glad to hear that restated because this procedure now suggested is not an amendment. It is a new resolution or it purports to be a new resolution. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce had not given notice in Votes and Proceedings but had said when we got back in committee, I propose to introduce an amendment to the proposed resolution, that would be an entirely different thing. However, that course is not being followed. With a proposed resolution already before us and in the possession of the committee, what it is sought to do here is to substitute for it a new and different resolution, not an amendment. This creates an entirely new situation and does not, in my submission, follow from the precedent with respect to bills upon which Your Honour based your argument this afternoon.
It is true that May at page 499, already referred to by Your Honour, does say:
There is no rule or custom which restrains the presentation of two or more bills relating to the same subject, and containing similar provision (s). But if a decision of the house has already been taken on one such bill, for example, if the bill has been given or refused a second reading, the other is not proceeded with if it contains substantially the same provisions,-
I should like to refer Your Honour back to page 383 in which it is said:
A motion must not anticipate a matter already appointed for consideration by the house, whether it be a bill or an adjourned debate upon a motion.
Here we have a motion on the order paper made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and which is being considered, that it is expedient to introduce a bill. That motion is now being considered in the committee of the whole. The Minister of Trade and Commerce proposes by the notice given in today's Votes and Proceedings another motion, not to amend the present one but to introduce a different one, both dealing with the same subject matter, and dealing with the subject matter of a motion already appointed for consideration by the house. Therefore, my first point is that here clearly within the meaning of May at page 383 we have a proposed motion which anticipates the matter of a motion upon the consideration of which the house has already embarked, and the further consideration of which is appointed for another day. That, I think, deals with the question of the difference between new resolutions and amendments.
Now, I go back to page 499 and the citation that you referred to which states that it is in order to introduce a new bill dealing with the same subject matter as another. May makes it clear that if a decision of the house has already been taken on one such bill, for example, then you could not introduce another bill. I submit that while it is not

Business of the House exactly on all fours, my proposition is largely the same; that when a decision of the house has already been taken with respect to the motion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce now on the order paper we have decided to commit that motion for consideration by the committee of the whole. That decision has been taken. It is true that the matter has not yet been finally disposed of, but we have had a decision of the house with respect to the motion, and now here we are with another motion coming along dealing with exactly the same thing and we are asked to take another decision. If that does not anticipate a motion already appointed for consideration, and if it does not seek to introduce a matter on which a decision of the house has already been taken, then I do not know the meaning of those words.
I believe that if Your Honour will read the two citations together, the one on page 499 and the one on page 383 to which I have referred you, you will see that there has to be something to reconcile the two which are otherwise in apparent conflict, and I believe I have suggested the only way in which they can be reconciled. That way is, firstly, it is not an amendment; it is a new motion. Secondly, it deals with something on which a decision of the house has already been taken because the house decided that the original motion is the one that should be referred to the committee of the whole. Now, the Minister of Trade and Commerce is asking us to decide that we were wrong then and it is some other motion that we should refer to the committee of the whole. That is my submission on the point that Your Honour has raised in answer to us.
Whatever may be Your Honour's decision you must recognize, sir, that we advance our point of view with vigour; we believe it to be correct. We may say, in the course of argument, we think it is so clear that a decision is obvious. Surely you will permit us to argue with vigour without saying we are reflecting upon you if your decision should happen to be the other way, however much we disagree with your decision.

subtopic: DR. CORLISS LAMONT-REFERENCE TO REFUSAL OF ENTRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. Could the minister report to the house, either now or later, on the refusal of immigration officers to admit to Canada Dr. Corliss Lamont who was to deliver lectures in the First Unitarian Church, Toronto, yesterday, and the grounds for such action by these officers?

subtopic: DR. CORLISS LAMONT-REFERENCE TO REFUSAL OF ENTRY
speechtext: Could the minister also say why he has changed his departmental mind?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
subtopic: DR. CORLISS LAMONT-REFERENCE TO REFUSAL OF ENTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the question relates to an individual case I think it is of sufficient public interest to make it desirable that a reply be made. I may say that Mr. Lamont arrived in Windsor yesterday. According to the information I have received from our Windsor office, before he arrived he advised the United Press, I am not sure whether in New York but at least somewhere in the United States, that he was coming to Canada to give some lectures. The United Press spoke to our office in Windsor and asked what would be done about him when he arrived.
It is quite probable that if these things had not happened there would have been no question raised about his entry into this country, but because these queries were made by the press, queries which perhaps in my suspicious mind might have been inspired by Mr. Lamont, certain questions were put to him. It appeared to the inquiry officer that he fell within the classes of person which parliament saw fit to prohibit entry to Canada under section 5 (1) of the Immigration Act which reads:
No person, other than a person referred to in subsection (2) of section 7, shall be admitted to Canada if he is a member of any of the following classes of persons:
(1) persons who are or have been, at any time before or after the commencement of this act, members of or associated with any organization, group or body of any kind concerning which there are reasonable grounds for believing that it promotes or advocates or at the time of such membership or association promoted or advocated subversion by force or other means of democratic government, institutions or processes, as they are understood in Canada, except persons who satisfy the minister that they have ceased to be members of or associated with such organizations, groups or bodies and whose admission would not be detrimental to the security of Canada.
In view of the information which was given to the inquiry officer by Mr. Lamont, and which indicated that he had at one time belonged to a certain organization which the attorney general of the United States had indicated was a subversive organization in that country, I have no criticism to make of the conscientious civil servant who ordered his deportation. Mr. Lamont was informed at once that he had a right of appeal to the minister. Up until a late hour last night he had not exercised that right, but I am told that he filed an appeal about midnight.
Early this morning I began to make inquiries about this matter which I confess had disturbed me. I found that an appeal had been entered and I took steps to see that

the material respecting the appeal was communicated to me in an unusually rapid way so that I could make a judgment upon it immediately. Upon considering the evidence in the case I could not satisfy myself that Mr. Lamont necessarily fell within the classes of persons mentioned in section 5 (1), and I accordingly decided to give him the benefit of the doubt and to allow his appeal.
I have been advised that he is on his way to Toronto to fulfil one of the two engagements. I took this course because it did not appear to me that, whatever the letter of the law might be, a lecture given by Mr. Lamont at the Unitarian church in Toronto would be the slightest danger to the security of Canada, and I did not think it was wise to have any unnecessary impression created that we in this country were afraid of listening to people like Mr. Lamont or that we were trying to suppress free speech. I think I might add, however, that it is my own belief, a belief which I doubt if I could support by concrete evidence, that this was a deliberate attempt on the part of a communist front organization to portray this country as a country in which we are afraid to allow free speech.

But if scientists, doctors or engineers were going to attend conventions where their own knowledge would be increased and thereby the technical knowledge and skills required in this country, which is apparently in need of them at the present time, it would not seem to me to be too difficult to iron out the matter. For instance, a regulation could be made in the department that they could not take any of their wives or families with them. I think that would help. Possibly there might be

some limitation on the expenses that could be deducted for conventions and such like. But simply to say that a certain incident-and that may be possible-prompted this legislation is rather shortsighted, in my opinion, in view of the need for trained scientists, engineers and doctors in this country. Since, as I believe I mentioned last evening, it is difficult to increase the numbers too quickly, the best we could possibly do is to try to increase the skills of those who are already there.
The discussion last evening, Mr. Chairman, seemed to revolve chiefly around the medical profession in particular. I would certainly agree that it is an extremely important profession. Advance in medicine might certainly be helped by our Canadian doctors attending conventions in the United States, South America and in Europe. I do not think any one would suggest that Canada is the sole repository of medical knowledge. A little later on in his remarks I believe the Minister of National Revenue suggested that if wealthy men go to these conventions, they should pay for it. I would quite agree that wealthy doctors, engineers and other scientists can well afford to go to conventions in other places. But by the time that men in the medical profession and in the other professions I have mentioned get to be wealthy they are usually fairly well on in years. It is the young scientists, the young doctors and the young engineers who are interested in getting this additional knowledge, not the old ones, or at least not to the same extent. If you want to encourage our young doctors, scientists and engineers to try to acquire knowledge in their fields and thus help not only themselves but this country when it is in need. I do not think the way to go about it is to discourage them in every way possible. Everyone knows that young doctors, and young scientists on staffs or working on their own often have families and have children to bring up; maybe there is a mortgage on the house to pay off. They have not enough money to go travelling even to fairly close parts of the United States. I think the government could very well help out by allowing any such scientist, engineer or doctor to go to two conventions a year, no matter where they might be, and allow their expenses, within certain financial limitations, as a deduction from income. Of course, this would not apply to their wives and families. I would agree with the remarks made last night in this respect by the Minister of National Revenue; that would certainly not be reasonable.
I cannot see why this restriction is placed in this resolution. As was pointed out by several hon. members last night, a doctor in Vancouver might want to attend a convention

in Halifax or in Quebec city, which is a long distance from Vancouver, and his expenses would be deductible. But if there were a convention in Buffalo a doctor living in Hamilton would not be able to deduct his expenses if he attended that convention, yet there would be little comparison between the two items of expense.
I should like to point out one other matter in this regard. A great many young scientists are on the staffs of our universities. Since they are salaried people, I understand from my colleagues who are accountants that they could not make a deduction of their expenses in attending conventions. However, their university could pay their expenses and allow them as a deduction. I think most of us realize, particularly in view of the news in the last few days that universities in Canada have had to raise their fees-which is a regrettable circumstance indeed-that most universities are not affluent. If the universities of this country wish to increase the knowledge of the scientists or engineers on their staffs, then the administrative bodies of the universities should be allowed to send these staff members abroad to gain that additional knowledge. The knowledge in all branches of science, like medicine, is certainly not confined to one country. I would hope that the Minister of Finance or his parliamentary assistant would give some kind of answer this afternoon to explain why there is this restriction, "in Canada", included in this resolution.

I must say, Mr. Chairman, I was rather disappointed a few minutes ago to observe that the Minister of Finance had apparently been called out of the house, because I certainly felt we should have had some reply from him to some of the questions that have been raised before this resolution is carried. I feel that some of the problems that were raised last night in respect to the inequities that, in my opinion, are going to be aggravated by the introduction of the proposal in section 2 of the resolution, do call for some explanation by the government as to why they are going to be allowed to continue. I recognize that the Minister of National Revenue did participate in the debate last night. But I would point out to you, as the minister so often and carefully explains to us, that the minister's function is an administrative one relating to the collection of taxes rather than to policy in regard to the imposition of taxes. His participation in the debate does not really constitute an answer from the government on the policy matters that have been raised.
In regard to the question of the discriminatory features that are in the present
Income Tax Act
section 5 of the act, which I suggested last night are going to be further aggravated by the proposal that is now before us, I mentioned that I had raised this particular matter last year and the year before. I recall that a year ago the parliamentary assistant did make some reply but his reply, in effect, was that he would draw my remarks to the attention of the minister. It would appear that if we get any reply on this matter it is going to be a somewhat similar reply from the parliamentary assistant. I would submit that on a matter which is as important as this, which affects many millions of Canadians, that sort of answer from the government is not good enough. For that reason I think we should expect some statement on these questions from the Minister of Finance which we could accept as a statement of the government's attitude or the government's policy on this matter.
If in their view discrimination does not exist, I for one would welcome some attempt on their part to explain why they take the view the act is not discriminatory now. It seems to me when one thinks of the situation I mentioned last night where you find an appeal being dismissed, and the judge who dismissed the appeal expressing such obvious sympathy with the plight of the appellant, as was the case in the situation to which I referred, that in itself should give us cause for considering the validity of the arguments I have been advancing. I know that it is all very well for me to go to the minister privately, as I did at the end of the last session, and get from him a straightforward private answer, which was really no explanation of policy. It is all very well for me to have to do that again this year, but I submit we have a right to expect some sort of explanation from the government or the Minister of Finance, who is charged with the responsibility of setting government policy on matters of this kind, before we are prepared to vote on the question that is now before us.

Before the parliamentary assistant answers, I want to repeat one suggestion I made last night. What is the objection to putting in the words "and the United States", making it Canada and the United States? If my argument last night that that would cost little or nothing was valid, and if the argument was valid that there may be a great balance of convenience in extending the scope of the measure to include south of the line, I ask the parliamentary assistant to give us an answer on that. I would further ask, if it is not possible for him to give us an affirmative answer today, would he at least say to us that this will be considered before the budget bill is introduced.

Income Tax Act

It is proposed here to restore more or less the administrative practice that had been in existence prior to 1855, when that court decision was rendered.
I understand that to mean they were simply reverting to the situation as it existed before. Was it not the practice of the department to allow medical people to attend one convention in the United States at that time?

In any event, he pointed out the difficulty from the administrative point of view of examining and deciding on the merits of exemptions of relatively small consequence in dollar amount. They involve a great deal of detail and cost in the examination of the individual tax returns, and so on.
The hon. member for Greenwood placed quite a specific question forward. He said he wondered why the words "United States" could not be very readily included in the resolution. Now, part of the thinking that restricts this to Canada is that the merit and advantages to the taxpayer from attendance at

The other is that most people, through their trade and professional associations, probably have some obligation in the matter of attending either a provincial or a national convention in Canada; but it is seldom that those obligations extend to the attending of conventions outside of Canada. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word on this matter. There are the chiropodists. Or Florida.

When he returned to my city a case came before him which he was able to cure. Mr. Chairman, I think the point brought out by the hon. member for Oxford and others relative to medical men is a sound and sensible one. For instance, in my own case my own dentist, who is a very able man in his profession, spends several weeks every year in New York, Chicago, or in some other centre attending clinics which he tells me are invaluable to him in keeping up with and abreast of the latest techniques in dentistry, and it makes a great deal of difference in the kind of treatment he is able to provide his patients. He also does considerable lecturing, and these trips are of great assistance to him in that regard.
As a businessman I have been able to travel extensively in the United States and
Income Tax Act
in other places to gain information for my company and I have been able to write off all expenses without any query. I can see no difference between that and trips made by medical men, scientists, engineers and so on, gaining information which is of great help to them in their professions. I do not think the government has given a satisfactory answer to this. The answer is simply: we do not want to do it, therefore we are not going to do it. Mr. Chairman, I just want to say a word or two about this. My understanding is-and I am reading from the ministers' budget speech at page 2332 of Hansard- that this resolution is really connected with and arises partly because of a supreme court decision known as the Home Oil case. The resolution itself strikes me as a rather amazing departure from the somewhat austere and matter-of-fact wording of resolutions because what we read here is:
That for the 1956 and subsequent taxation years uncertainty regarding the applicability of outstanding regulations respecting depletion allowances be removed.
I would have thought that that could only happen in another and better world but nevertheless it is desirable to have a high objective. It does prompt me to say, however, that the resolution as worded sounds more like a prayer than a resolution.
Now coming back to the references made to the Home Oil case, I read from the minister's speech:
The reasons for judgment given by the court in the Home Oil case have created some uncertainty as to whether the present law and regulations as amended in 1951 are in sufficiently clear terms to support assessments made since 1951. It is proposed, therefore, to amend the law and regulations now to ensure that the intent of the 1951 amendment shall govern for the intervening period

and for the future. This amendment will not deprive any taxpayer of his rights under the supreme court decision for the years prior to 1951.
I take it that the parliamentary assistant will say something on this by way of explanation of the problem which is arising in the minds of oil producers between 1951 and 1956 and I also hope that he will just say a word about the terms of the Home Oil decision so that we may have on the record an explanation of the situation which prompts this resolution.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It will be noted by the house that it is now proposed that this amendment to the law and regulations shall date from 1956 and not from 1951, which was mentioned in the speech made by the minister as found at page 2332 of Hansard.
As originally announced, it was intended to make this amendment date from 1951 so there would be no uncertainty in the period from 1951 to the present. It was never intended to deprive the taxpayer of his rights under the supreme court decision for the years prior to 1951. However, representations have been made since the budget speech from which my hon. friend quoted to the effect that amending the law effective to 1951 would deprive taxpayers of the right to test the validity of the law and regulations as they now stand and have stood for the period from 1951 to the present and accordingly it is now proposed that the amendment shall date from 1956 only.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a question or two to the parliamentary assistant on this particular subject. He states that by this proposed amendment he hopes to clarify some misunderstanding on the part of oil operators and others as to what the department actually means by depletion.
I presume what the department intends to do is to carry on in the future the same general policy followed by the department over the last several years, and that in effect is this: a statement to Canadian oil companies that if they want depletion on their oil producing properties they must quit exploring; however, if they want to gain the benefits of depletion allowance on their producing properties all they have to do is quit exploring for oil and let the exploration job be done by someone else.
It is a fact, sir, that as the regulations are now administered very few-as a matter of fact, less than one-tenth of Canadian oil companies-draw any benefit whatsoever from the depletion allowance. It is also true that while the act or the regulations would indicate a depletion allowance of one-third of

net profit is allowed on producing properties, in actual fact benefit from depletion for Canadian oil companies has amounted to less than 1 per cent of the revenue derived from producing properties.
The great question of Canadian policy with regard to depletion has been the cause of a great deal of concern not only to oil companies but also to governments and the general public of this country. For example, I find that the views I have expressed on this particular subject from time to time over the last three years are fully supported by the government of the province of Saskatchewan, a government which, as a socialist government, might normally be considered as one opposed to any form of tax hand-out, if you want to call depletion that, to private corporations. Yet we have a statement by Hon. J. H. Brockelbank, minister of natural and mineral resources of Saskatchewan, which appeared in the Western Oil Examiner of January 15 last. Mr. Brockelbank had this to say:
Another important point is that due to a special tax concession to risk investment capital in the United States, the American oil and gas industry has enjoyed an advantage over Canadian risk capital in the same field. In coming to Canada, the American oil industry has spent dollars which otherwise would have found their way into the American treasury.
These dollars, although welcome in Canada, have placed the Canadian investment dollar at a considerable disadvantage because of unequal dollar responsibility.
In its submission to the Gordon royal commission the Saskatchewan government went a little further than that. I think the comments made at that time might appropriately be read into the record of this house. The brief of the Saskatchewan government had this to say:
The second general question to which the attention of the commission is drawn concerns what appears to be the continuing hesitancy on the part of Canadians and Canadian companies to invest freely in the development of their national assets. The great resources boom that has played such a prominent part in the post-war expansion in the Canadian economy stems in large measure from the substantial inflow of foreign capital, first from the United States and latterly from the United Kingdom and western Europe.
This has been as true in Saskatchewan as in other provinces, especially in oil exploration where non-resident capital has played the major development role. The inflow of capital has made, and will undoubtedly continue to make, a valued and lasting contribution to the growth of the provincial economy. At the same time it would be highly desirable to secure a more active and expanded participation by Canadians and Canadian capital in this growth. Among the problems mentioned by Canadian companies in this connection, however, is the fact that under the combined impact of United States and Canadian federal income tax laws and regulations, the American-owned companies operating in this country enjoy
Income Tax Act
a competitive tax advantage over Canadian companies. If it is the policy of the federal government to encourage the fullest possible participation and ownership of resources by Canadian capital in the expansion of the domestic economy, a careful review and action to remove any competitive disabilities suffered by Canadian companies should be suggested.
The government of Alberta, which of course is a Social Credit administration, made even stronger representations in connection with this particular phase of the Canadian tax policy to the Gordon royal commission. In his statement to that commission the premier of Alberta was quite clear that the government of Alberta supported the idea of the inflow of foreign capital to that province, which of course has meant hundreds of millions of dollars for the provincial treasury, but at the same time it was said that the government of Alberta would like to see a much greater participation by Canadian companies and Canadian investors. It was suggested that the best way of achieving this would be by a revision of the Canadian tax laws in order to create actually workable and effective depletion allowances much along the lines of those applied under the United States law to all companies in the United States, whether they carry out their spendings in the United States or anywhere else in the world.
The Conservative party has put its views on record in connection with this important matter, and they have been on record for a long time. However, last January the national Conservative association of Canada decided to go a step further and put on the formal record its views on the matter of Canadian tax laws, particularly with regard to depletion. The following resolution was approved by the national Conservative association:
Whereas it is in the national interest that Canadians be encouraged to participate to the maximum in the development and ownership of Canadian natural resources such as oil and gas and other minerals;
We urge the Canadian government to amend the Income Tax Act, particularly in regard to depletion allowance and lease acquisition cost write-offs in order that Canadians may compete on a nearer to equal competitive basis in the acquisition and development of Canadian oil and gas and other minerals with Americans who have the advantage of United States tax law provisions.
These things I have read indicate pretty clearly that no matter where the political views of Canadians happen to lie as between a socialist or Social Credit provincial government or the Conservative party of Canada, all are agreed on one thing, that our Canadian tax laws discriminate against Canadian investment in the development of Canadian resources.
Before going any further perhaps I should examine the question of just what is a

Income Tax Act
depletion allowance. Depletion allowances are basically and simply the recognition that an oil well or a mine producing any form of mineral, be it coal, gold, iron or any other, is a wasting asset, is something strictly limited as to the ultimate production which will be yielded. In order to stay permanently in business the owner must continuously *explore to replace the reserves that are produced. In principle, depletion allowances provide natural resources production industries with a lower rate of taxation than other industries which do not have the same problem of replacing by exploration the products they produce. Depletion does not apply to what might be termed the normal business phases of such an industry as the crude oil industry. In other words the profits from refining or marketing the oil are taxed at the full corporate tax rate without benefit of any depletion allowance.
Under the present Canadian policy, a policy which has prevailed for some years, those operating oil and gas wells are extended a depletion allowance of 334 Per cent of the net profits, if any, remaining after all the costs of exploration and development have been recovered. However, because the huge expenditures in recent years have far exceeded the gross production income, only about one-tenth of the Canadian companies engaged in exploration have been in a position to make any net production income against which to apply a depletion allowance. The actual benefit of depletion allowances so far has only been about 1 per cent of the spendings made to replace and increase crude reserves. Therefore the purposes of the depletion provisions have been largely defeated.
Under the present regulations a Canadian company could discover an oil or gas field, and if it were carrying on active exploration work it could produce all the oil or gas from that pool and receive very little if any in the way of depletion allowance. On the other hand, if that company decided to halt or reduce its exploration work it could derive a substantial depletion allowance on the ultimate profits from the operation of that field. There is thus a penalty imposed under the Canadian tax laws upon any company willing to continue large-scale exploration, and that is a most undesirable thing in a nation whose future depends in no small measure upon the continued risking of large amounts of capital on natural resources exploration and development.
In contrast to the limited application of the depletion provisions to Canadian companies which pay out a large part of the exploration development costs in western Canada, there

is under the present tax policy a depletion allowance of 25 per cent of gross income extended to the recipients of gross and net royalty interests in Canadian oil and gas wells. In other words those who do not take part in the exploration costs of the oil and have a royalty interest in the production of individual wells are entitled to the full 25 per cent gross depletion allowance. This is allowed to many farmers and others who own mineral rights, and is a much greater depletion allowance than is allowed under the Canadian law to Canadian companies who are bearing the entire cost of exploring and developing these products.
I have suggested in the house at various times in the past that the government should amend its present depletion allowance regulations to provide that the present allowance of 25 per cent of gross production income now permitted to royalty owners in Canada be extended also to those who provide the costs of exploration and development, and that we should use this gross depletion allowance in place of the current allowance of a so-called 334 per cent of any ultimate net profits. Such a step would go a long way toward providing a continuing incentive for Canadian capital to maintain a large-scale exploration program in Canada. In addition, it would also put the Canadian in a more nearly equal position to his competitor, the American, in the drive to develop Canadian resources.
I might say that under United States law United States companies have a choice of the most beneficial to them of two depletion methods. They can either take 27J per cent on gross production income by way of depletion, or else they may take 50 per cent of net production income for depletion. The proposal I make that our depletion should be 25 per cent of gross production income is still not nearly as generous as that provided under United States law.
In addition to depletion on oil and gas wells, we do have in Canada depletion on our other mineral resources, and there seems to be no consistency whatsoever in the departments's application or determination of the principle of depletion. For example, base and precious metal mines are allowed a depletion allowance of 334 per cent of their annual profits. In the case of gold mines they are allowed a depletion allowance of either 40 per cent of their profits each year or else a depletion allowance of $4 per ounce of gold produced in that year. In the case of industrial mineral mines dealing with non-bedded deposits we have a depletion allowance of 334 per cent of the profits in each year. In the case of coal mines we have a straight depletion of 10 cents per ton for

each ton of coal mined in any given year. There are also in the case of certain types of mines special allowances by way of tax concessions.
But in each of these other mineral industries we have a situation somewhat different from that applying to the oil and gas industry. In the case of a metal mine or a coal mine we do not have the operator of that mine faced with the necessity of huge capital expenditures on exploration and development. In the case of oil particularly the companies, big or small, if they are going to stay successfully in business, must gamble up to many times the gross amount of income they can hope to receive from their properties that are producing at the present time, and the ratio of moneys they must expend for oil exploration compared with their production income is far higher than in the case of base metals or precious metals.
It has been pointed out very ably by a great many executives of various companies, big and small, including executives of United States oil companies, at the recent Gordon commission hearings that we in Canada make it tougher for Canadians to take part in their own resource development by making our depletion regulations in Canada somewhat tougher than those applying in the case of our American brethren. For example, here is a statement made on March 28 at the annual meeting of Canadian Oil Companies Limited, which I believe is the largest single wholly Canadian-owned integrated oil company. Harold Rea, president of Canadian Oil Companies Limited, had this to say:
The Canadian tax structure .	.	. gives non-
Canadians distinct competitive advantage in our own oil fields.
He went on to say:
Canadian crude oil must compete with foreign crude, but it is at a disadvantage in such competition if it is developed and produced in a tax climate less favourable than in other countries.
He concluded by saying:
We risk and lose one hundred cents on every dollar on the cost of unproductive acreage. United States companies risk only the net cost after deducting income tax.
The practical effect, so far as western Canada is concerned, is that there has been an increasing percentage of the proved and potential oil and gas lands of the west going into the hands of foreign companies. That is something we in the west do not blame on the United States oil companies because the fault largely lies right here in Canada, and I believe lies largely in the hands of the federal income tax department. By our policies, particularly with respect to depletion and certain other
Income Tax Act
phases of taxation, we have placed our Canadian companies at a very serious disadvantage in the development of our own Canadian resources.
I may say, sir, that there have been a number of Canadian independent oil companies that have developed in recent years and have done a fairly successful job of growing. But when we examine how they have grown we find that they have grown despite Canadian tax law, not because of any assistance from it. For example, some of our independent Canadian oil companies have been able to expand because they have had men in charge of them who were smart enough to go into new areas in the west ahead of the major companies, and were able to take by reservation large blocks of land. At a subsequent date, when the area became hotter than ever, they were able to make deals with the larger American companies as a result of which these American firms spent money for the exploration of these Canadian companies' lands with a share of the profits going to the Canadian company without the Canadian company being obligated to spend large sums on exploration. That has been one road to success for some Canadian companies, and I hope that road remains open.
Another road to success for some of our Canadian oil companies has been in drilling contracting, in other words going into some of the more normal phases of business and doing work for other companies, carrying out seismograph surveys, drilling oil wells and so on, on a contract basis and earning normal profits which supplement their earning capacity very largely and make it a little easier for them to get into the main job of exploring for and developing oil resources.
Then we have another method that some Canadian companies have followed, namely by going into refining or marketing. Some Canadian companies have been quite successful in that regard despite the stiff competition existing in those fields.
The fourth method by which some Canadian companies have endeavoured to stay alive and grow has been one forced on them, one which I am confident is very detrimental to the interests of this country, namely that of doing the reverse of what the United States companies have been doing. Where American companies have been coming into Canada, we find that Canadian companies have been setting up United States subsidiaries to spend their good Canadian money exploring for and developing oil and gas in the United States in order to gain the advantage of the tax laws of that country. I may say that in recent years there has been an outflow of tens of millions of dollars of Canadian oil money into

Income Tax Act
the northern United States, Texas and Oklahoma for the development of United States oil and gas resources because the tax climate in the United States is far more favourable than it has been and still is in Canada.
I would much prefer, and I am sure these Canadian oil companies would too, to see these dollars spent here in Canada in order to give Canadians a bigger share in their own natural resources. When the government brings in its amendment to the depletion regulations I would strongly recommend that it should not simply try to impose on a firm basis the interpretation of depletion that it had been applying or attempting to apply for some years, an interpretation which the Supreme Court of Canada threw out; but that in place of that it revise its depletion regulations in order to give Canadians and Canadian companies a far better break, to encourage greater Canadian participation in the development of some of our vital Canadian resources.

Mr. Chairman, I should like briefly to support the argument which has just been made by my colleague the hon. member for Calgary South. I was extremely glad that the retroactive features of this legislation-which the budget address of the Minister of Finance indicated would be imposed-have now been withdrawn. However, I think we are still in the position that the depletion provisions of our Income Tax Act which are designed to be incentive legislation, are not acting as they were intended to act. As I understand the thing, their reason for being there is in order to give incentive to people to put money into exploration for oil and gas to develop that industry.
The nub of the matter is that they are not acting in the way they were intended to act because of the way they are applied. I think the matter is summed up concisely in the brief of the Canadian Petroleum Association to the royal commission on Canada's economic future which was presented on February 17, 1956. I should just like to read a paragraph from it concerning this matter:
The Canadian Petroleum Association submits that the motive behind the present provisions of the Income Tax Act and regulations whereby the operator of an oil or gas well is allowed to deduct 331 per cent of net profits as depletion or risk allowance was to provide the needed financial stimulus to enable the operator to use receipts from production for further exploration and development and still be able to pay a return to the shareholder. However, we also submit that the purpose of the allowance is largely defeated when Canadian producers, now in competition with foreign producers, must first deduct exploration expenditures before making this calculation. Indeed you might say that under the existing regulations the prudent operator is actually discouraged from the re-risking of his profit. This allowance, if properly applied, should result in more money being put back into exploration than would be
[Mr. Nickle.l
possible without it. In this way, the efficient operator not only would have the incentive but also the necessary substantial financial boost to keep him interested in taking the risk involved in the search for oil. The chance of having a greater margin after tax would induce both investor and speculator to support our oil and gas industry. With that incentive more sums would be risked, and more lost, but the search would continue.
If we are to have this legislation for an incentive purpose, in order to encourage the search for oil, why not have it in a form which will accomplish that purpose? What is the use of having it in a form which does not accomplish what the legislation is designed to do? I would therefore also strongly urge the Minister of Finance to reconsider this matter and put this depletion allowance on a basis which will enable it to do what it was intended to do, namely encourage the search for oil and at the same time place Canadian operators in a much better position, vis-a-vis United States operators, than they are in at the present time.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. I want to draw the attention of the parliamentary assistant again to the very unusual nature of this resolution. It really gives us nothing definite to bite on. Paragraphs 1 and 2, of course, are quite definite. We know exactly what we are talking about. We have just now heard a powerful comment on this theory of taxation. Before we pass this resolution it would seem to me that we should have a great deal more than we have now. It seems to me that we should have the government's decision as to the whole depletion policy. Surely that would not be unreasonable.
The minister has candidly told us that he is holding over the excise resolution because he has a certain conclusion still to arrive at there. I submit that this might be usefully done here. We have heard this situation reviewed by a man of admitted knowledge in the field. We have heard the statements he has made as to the disadvantages under which Canadian explorers labour. Certainly they are widely believed. The department may have an answer satisfactory to them, but there is no doubt that they are widely believed. There has been more than one submission to the Gordon commission along that line. I ran across one the other day from Husky Oil by a man called Neilson. I think he is a man of standing in the industry.
This resolution at the present time merely expresses, as I say, a pious hope that uncertainty be removed. It is desirable, of course. But what is desirable before we decide is that we know what it is we want to make

certain. We have not been able to discuss that matter today at all. All we have by way of material is the Home Oil case. Then we have had what I submit is a formidable criticism by the hon. member for Calgary South. I do not imagine it would be reasonable to ask the government to submit the matter to the banking and commerce committee, but I suggest that it might well warrant further consideration and an income tax resolution, as I said a moment or two ago, sufficiently definite so that we may have a real debate on the question.
As the matter stands now, if nothing further is given to us it seems to me that this will go back to the government without any further suggestions, without any possibility of our criticizing what the government has in mind because, so far as I am aware, we do not know what it is. I have put this suggestion to the parliamentary assistant before he replies in the hope that it may be accepted as a reasonable and practical one likely to give us the necessary material so we can discuss it at the resolution stage.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I really do not think my friend the hon. member for Greenwood has any uncertainty about the word "uncertainty" that is referred to in this resolution. In speaking to the resolution he indicated that he had fully reread the remarks of the minister in the budget speech when the minister explained the nature of the uncertainty that was to be corrected this session.
Although there are only two paragraphs, I do not think it is necessary to read what the minister had to say as reported at page 2332 of Hansard of March 20. It was clear that he was attempting to leave no legal uncertainty as to the regulations or the intent of the government with respect to depletion allowances, even though the Home Oil court case may have created some uncertainty in the minds of certain people.
As to the broader argument with respect to depletion that has been advanced by the hon. member for Calgary South, may I say that I have every respect for his broad and special knowledge of the petroleum industry. However, I think he will agree with me that the content of his speech today varies little from the speeches he has made advocating similar policies not only last year but in previous sessions.
All I can say is that last year, on June 2, the Minister of Finance explained government policy with respect to depletion for the petroleum industry. He did that in answer to similar arguments that have been made here by both the hon. member for Calgary South,
Income Tax Act
and the hon. member for Greenwood, who read editorial comment at the time from the Montreal Gazette. This comment was in support of an argument such as has been advanced again today by the hon. member for Calgary South.
Now, I think everyone who has spoken on this subject of depletion in the petroleum industry has made reference to the Gordon economic commission. Naturally those who advocate changes in the tax laws with respect to depletion allowances in the petroleum industry have quoted from associations that have come before that commission and advocated something similar to their own views. I am not particularly going to take the other side today, because the Minister of Finance outlined his views last year. He received representations along this line again this year, and came to the conclusion that it was not desirable to change the present law with respect to depletion, except to the extent he mentioned in his budget speech at page 2332 of Hansard.
In the meantime, since the last budget we have had the Gordon commission. As I have said, one of the matters about which many representations have been made to the commission is this matter of the depletion allowance in the petroleum industry. The minister came to the conclusion that this year he would not make any changes in the situation with respect to depletion pending some report that might come from this commission. Now, inasmuch as some quotations have been made from briefs presented to this commission, I think it is only fair that I might say there are two views on this subject, just as there are usually on anything else. I myself recently picked up in the press a comment on a submission that had been made by the Bailey Selburn Oil and Gas Company to the Gordon economic commission. They said:
We believe that aggressive Canadian companies are well able to hold their place and have had a fair opportunity to do so.
I also note that one of our eminent accountants, Mr. J. G. Glassco, made representations to the Gordon commission and presented another view that has not been mentioned with respect to the United States investment, and I think it had a particular bearing on the investments that have been made in the Canadian oil fields. He is reported as having said in his brief:
The great majority of the recent increase in foreign investment in Canada has come from the United States and the taxation pattern in that country, particularly since 1950, has provided strong incentives to the investment of capital in other countries.
Reenactment of the United States excess profits tax at the time of the Korean war in 1950, and in force until 1953, brought about a situation where

Income Tax Act
profits taxable at rates as high as 82 per cent could he used to blot up preliminary losses resulting from development of new business. A good deal of such money found its way into Canada, particularly in the case of the petroleum industry.
That is what we are arguing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
My hon. friend may present some aspects of United States tax law that may be more favourable to those engaged in the petroleum industry than might exist in Canada. On the other hand, I would point out to him that there are many features that are of advantage to corporate taxpayers in Canada who are engaged in the petroleum industry that do not apply to somebody similarly engaged in the United States. I refer to the fact that our corporate tax rate is lower than that in the United States. I refer to the fact that the dividend tax credit allowance was introduced in Canada prior to its introduction in the United States. Those are all factors that, of course, are not brought out when the argument is one-sided.
But I do assure my hon. friends that this matter of depletion was again considered this year, and for the reasons I have indicated, particularly because of the economic study, it was not thought any radical changes should be made beyond those that are contained in the budget resolution. I suggest to my hon. friend there is no uncertainty about the limitations contained in that resolution, because they are outlined in the budget speech.

First of all, since the parliamentary assistant has quoted from the Bailey Selburn brief to the Gordon commission, I would say that I happen to have a copy of it here. I did mention in the course of my earlier remarks that a number of Canadian independent companies had been able to go along successfully by the use of devious routes other than the policies laid down by the tax department. Bailey Selburn is one of those which have been notably successful by the use of methods outside the tax policy which I mentioned in my remarks.
The Bailey Selburn brief to the Gordon royal commission, after pointing out that they had been able to succeed by other means than the tax policy in Canada, came out very strongly in favour of amending the Canadian tax laws. Their final submission to the Gordon commission was this:
It is our opinion that amendments should be made in taxation regulations to permit:
(a)	A fair deduction for depletion of reserves on a gross production basis;
(b)	That lease costs be allowed as write-offs;
(c)	That moneys expended in drilling and exploration be deductible items for individuals and businesses in Canada where losses occur.

In other words Bailey Selburn, the outfit you have mentioned, joined with the rest of the industry in suggesting a change in the depletion laws.
The parliamentary assistant has said that since we have the Gordon commission and the Gordon commission is receiving a great many briefs on this subject and is going to come to some conclusion in the near future, perhaps we should not bother changing our policy on depletion now. Would it not be best, sir, to drop this amendment altogether and let the depletion law of Canada be that which the Supreme Court of Canada decided in the Home Oil case was the intention of parliament back in 1949? In other words, let us have in Canada well by well depletion, as the supreme court said was the intention of parliament in that Home Oil case.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Would my hon. friend say that has been the law since the regulation of 1951?

The parliamentary assistant refers to the amendments made in 1951, which the minister now wishes to alter in order to avoid the chance that the Supreme Court of Canada will rule the 1951 amendment has exactly the same intent as the 1949 amendment. In other words the department obviously feels the Supreme Court of Canada will rule that in the amendment of 1951 parliament intended well by well depletion, and not this present policy of the department which rules that if you are going to spend money on exploration you cannot have depletion.
I would strongly suggest, sir, that we drop the amendment altogether and leave the law as it stands until we get a recommendation from the Gordon royal commission. In his answers last June 2, the Minister of Finance stated that a change in the depletion law was not necessary because we did not have a capital gains tax in Canada which, I presume, was one of those advantages under Canadian law that did not apply under United States tax law, where a capital gains tax does exist.
Sir, would the parliamentary assistant please explain to me how the absence of a so-called capital gains tax in Canada offers any benefit to the company whose purpose is to go out to explore for, develop and produce oil and gas? Surely the parliamentary assistant is not suggesting that the Canadian oil company makes its profit out of production by spending its money for exploration, then developing production and selling it presumably to the Americans or to anyone else, in order to realize a profit on production that it cannot realize under the existing tax policy of his department.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As to the latter point, Mr. Chairman, the reference to capital gains, of course, is a broad reference. My hon. friend did advance the argument that Canadians were discouraged from making investments, and particularly in their resources, because of discouraging tax laws. Certainly the absence of a capital gains tax in Canada is of advantage to investors in the natural resources of the country.

It may be that I emphasized too much the wording of paragraph 3, but I did think there had been certain recent events which possibly create a situation where this thing might have another look taken at it. speechtext:
