I have heard part of what he said from time to time; I am quite satisfied with it. The hon. member for Calgary South ought to bear in mind that what we are doing here is restoring what we consider is government policy. We are not going further than that. We are merely putting government taxation back to where we thought it was before the Home Oil decision was given. Therefore to that extent he ought to be content.
If the Gordon commission makes a recommendation I am sure it will receive careful consideration. In fact I will go further and repeat what I am sure the parliamentary assistant has already said. I assured the members of this business, when they saw me two weeks ago, that the whole subject which I know is under discussion at the moment, would be considered again before the next session of parliament; but it was on the assumption that' by that time the Gordon commission would have reported. If it does not, it will be given another consideration. I think my hon. friend ought to accept the situation that the government would at' this session put the law back to what it thought it was, and leave the major decision as to whether there ought to be a change for full consideration which could not be given at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I gather then the decision is going to be something like this.

Income Tax Act
With regard to depletion for the production years 1949 and 1950 we have the definition of the Supreme Court of Canada of depletion policy which will apply. For the years 1951 to 1955, inclusive, we have the definition of depletion very much in doubt, in as much as so far no assessments have been made on oil companies for those years, and therefore it has not' been possible for oil companies to appeal to the courts for a definition of depletion as applied by the tax department for those years. For 1956 we will have presumably a new clear-cut definition of government policy on depletion, but it may be that in 1957 we shall have still a fourth policy based, I hope, upon recommendations to be made by the Gordon commission. We would then have at least three different depletion policies; one certain, 1949 and 1950; one uncertain, 1951 to 1955; and 1956, certain, presumably; and after 1956, most uncertain. Would it not be best in that interim period of 1956 to leave the law as it has been defined by the supreme court and then, after getting the Gordon commission report, review the matter next year?

I know it would be the act of a lazy man to follow the advice of my hon. friend and leave things as they are, but I think it ought-

speechtext: There is an amendment here. The proposal now is to delete this item.

speechtext: This proposed tariff item would incorporate two temporary tariff items covering engines and parts of power lawn mowers. It is a tidying-up operation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
As the result of a tariff board declaration dated since budget night, namely April 6 this year, tools which have been made to fit specific machines or specific attachments will no longer be classified under the item covering tools, but instead they will be classified as "parts" of such machines or attachments. This will have the effect of reducing the duty on many of these tools which are of a class made in Canada from 22J per cent to 7J per cent.
The wording of the new item makes it clear that these tools, even though they may be made for use in particular machines or particular attachments, will be dutiable at 22J per cent under the most favoured nation tariff if they are of a class made in Canada. Only with respect to such tools of a class not made in Canada will the duty be 7J per cent.

stagedirection
speechtext: The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

speakerposition: topic

speechtext:
At the recent meeting of the dominion council of health, did the Minister of National Health and Welfare discuss with the provincial representatives present the federal proposal on hospital insurance?
Answer by: Hon. Paul Martin (Minister of
National Health and Welfare):
As the dominion council of health is largely made up of technical officers of the federal and provincial health departments it is not in a position to deal with matters of policy that are under study by the governments concerned. However, the Minister of National Health and Welfare did take advantage of the opportunity presented by the recent meeting of the dominion council of health to indicate to the provincial representatives present the importance which the government attached to the recent federal proposal respecting hospital insurance and laboratory and radiological diagnostic services.

Thursday, May 10, 1956
